stops.name: Frankfurt, Gruner's Musterschule: the calling strikes
stops.campa: In the early summer of 1805 Fröbel enters Frankfurt to train as an architect, and a friend introduces him to Anton Gruner, headmaster of the new Model School. Fröbel speaks openly of his life and its object, and Gruner, reading him at a glance, pronounces the sentence that turns the hinge of the century's pedagogy. Days later the omen seals it: his testimonials, the architect's credentials, the Jena certificates, are lost in transit, no one ever learns how. Fröbel reads it plainly: Providence itself has torn up the old papers. He accepts the teacher's place. The architect is dead; the educator is born.
stops.quote: 'Oh,' said Gruner, turning to me, 'give up architecture; it is not your vocation at all. Become a teacher. We want a teacher in our own school. Say you agree, and the place shall be yours.'
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the first lesson: the fish in the water
stops.campa: He stands for the first time before a class, thirty or forty boys of nine to eleven, to teach arithmetic, drawing, geography, German. And the thing happens that happens to the called: the room closes around him like a native element. That same week he writes to his brother that he has found what he never knew yet always missed. Every wandering year, every survey chain and account book, is redeemed in a single hour. From this classroom he never really departs; everything afterwards is its enlargement downward, toward younger and younger children, until it reaches the cradle.
stops.quote: It seemed as if I had found something I had never known, but always longed for, always missed, as if my life had at last discovered its native element. I felt as happy as the fish in the water, the bird in the air.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827); letter to his brother, 1805

stops.name: Yverdon, the first pilgrimage to Pestalozzi
stops.campa: Towards the end of August 1805, before he has taught a full month, Gruner's new master is already on the road to Yverdon, where Pestalozzi has lately raised his standard in the lakeside castle. Received kindly, turned loose in the classrooms, the inexperienced pilgrim watches for a fortnight and comes away shaken and kindled at once: elevated and depressed, aroused and bewildered. He senses that heart and mind would come to grief if he stayed longer now; he is not yet strong enough for this fire. He carries the teaching-plan home like an ember wrapped in cloth.
stops.quote: What I saw was to me at once elevating and depressing, arousing and also bewildering.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, return with the ember
stops.campa: In mid-October 1805 he is back at the Model School with his definite appointment from the Consistorium and a settled vow to return to Yverdon for a longer stay. He throws himself into the reorganisation of the whole school upon Pestalozzian lines, teaching by the new method, testing it against thirty living boys at a time. Two years he serves here, the Swiss flame banked in a Frankfurt stove. When consulted on matters he has never studied, he looks within and to Nature for the answer, and the answer gladdens the inquirer.
stops.quote: I left Yverdon in mid-October (1805) with a settled resolution to return thither as soon as possible for a longer stay.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Holzhausen Oede: tutor of three boys
stops.campa: Caroline von Holzhausen gives him her three sons entire, and Fröbel leaves the school to become their tutor, moving with the boys out to the family's garden estate, the Oede, before the gates of the city. Here he makes his first whole experiment: education not by lessons alone but by a shared life: garden work, walks, the day itself as teacher. He learns what a family is from inside one, he the motherless man in a mother's household; and he learns that his three pupils are not enough school for him. All four of them must go to Pestalozzi.

stops.name: Yverdon, arrival with the three pupils
stops.campa: In 1808 tutor and pupils travel together to Yverdon and settle in the shadow of the castle, lodging at its very gates when the castle itself is refused them, to live for two years inside Pestalozzi's experiment as scholars among the scholars. Fröbel comes expecting everything; he takes the boys to the common meals, the common lessons, the whole common life. He has arrived at the master's side at the flood-tide of the institute, and he means to receive the flame whole: not the methods only, but the love beneath the methods.
stops.quote: With such expectations I arrived at Yverdon. There was no educational problem whose resolution I did not firmly expect to find there.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Yverdon, the master's flame: evenings on the lake shore
stops.campa: A year deep in the work, Fröbel walks each evening from the schoolrooms to the hills and the shore of Lake Neuchâtel, and the walks become liturgy: sunset on the glaciers, the pine forests bathed in rosy light, Pestalozzi's evening addresses on noble manhood still sounding in him. Nature herself, unsought, draws the walkers close. Here he first thinks systematically of his brother's children in Thuringia, and begins extracting and classifying everything at Yverdon that a family could use: the Keilhau institute drafted, unknowingly, on the shore of a Swiss lake.
stops.quote: As I wandered on the sunlit, far-stretching hills, or along the still shore of the lake, clear as crystal, smooth as a mirror, or in the shady groves, under the tall forest trees, my spirit grew full with ideas of the truly god-like nature and priceless value of a man's soul.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Yverdon, farewell to Pestalozzi
stops.campa: In 1810 the discipleship completes itself the only way true discipleship can: by departure. Fröbel has seen the glory of the institute and also its wound: the want of inner unity, of organic ground-principle beneath the methods; all that is good and all that is imperfect at Yverdon have alike become his teachers. He takes his pupils home by Bern, Schaffhausen and Stuttgart, resolved to equip himself at a German university with the natural science an educator must have. He carries the master's flame away in a vessel the master never possessed: the idea of law-governed development.
stops.quote: On the whole I passed a glorious time at Yverdon, elevated in tone, and critically decisive for my after life.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Göttingen, languages, sciences, and the law of the sphere
stops.campa: At Göttingen the returned disciple sets out to read the universe from both ends: ancient languages to reach the childhood of mankind, natural sciences to reach the law of its growth. In solitary walks he arrives at his great simplification: one law of development running unbroken from stone through plant to the human soul, the spherical law in which every particular unfolds the whole. What he traced at Göttingen amid outward circumstances, confirming the order of the soul's development, he will soon find written a hundredfold in stone. Chemistry and physics point him onward: to Berlin, to the crystals.

stops.name: Berlin, crystallography under Weiss
stops.campa: In October 1812 Fröbel comes to Berlin to sit under Christian Samuel Weiss, the great crystallographer. The lectures he has longed for answer him exactly: in the fixed forms of crystals he sees demonstrated the inner connection of the whole cosmical development of the universe: diversity forever unfolding within unity. The crystal is the child's future Gifts prefigured in stone: sphere, cube, law-formed unfolding. To hold himself at the university he teaches in a Berlin school, and finds he can now turn his thoughts once more to educational problems, armed.
stops.quote: The lectures for which I had so longed really came up to the needs of my mind and soul, and awakened in me, more fervent than ever, the certainty of the demonstrable inner connection of the whole cosmical development of the universe.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Berlin, the call to arms: the teacher's reason for war
stops.campa: The fateful year 1813 opens; all Prussia grasps weapons against Napoleon. Fröbel is no Prussian and owns, he says, a Motherland rather than a Fatherland; yet he enlists, and for a reason no soldier ever gave before him: every child he might one day educate will have a Fatherland, and the man who declined to defend it with his blood could never stand unashamed before a child again. His enthusiasm is small, his determination fixed as rock. It is the first article of the pedagogy, written before the pedagogy: the teacher must be whole before the children.
stops.quote: Every boy, that every child, who might perhaps later on come to be educated by me would have a Fatherland, that this Fatherland was now requiring defence, and that the child was not in a position to share in that defence.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)

stops.name: Dresden, Eastertide muster of the Lützowers
stops.campa: At Eastertide 1813 Fröbel reaches Dresden on his way to the black-uniformed infantry of Lützow's Free Corps. Among the crowds of vigorous volunteers, many of them Berlin students like himself, the self-concentrated scholar knows not one man. He has chosen the Lützowers because they fight for no single crown but for a pure German brotherhood, the ideal he has honoured in his soul as lofty and sublime. The weak-bodied naturalist shoulders a musket among strangers, trusting the campaign to furnish what his whole life has lacked: brothers.
stops.quote: As comrades I selected the Luetzowers; and at Eastertide 1813 I arrived at Dresden on my road to join the infantry division of Luetzow's corps.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Friedrich Froebel (letter to the Duke of Meiningen, 1827)
